families.s: HSE glass and glazing handling, cutting and installation safety guidance
families.t: sharp edges, breakage, lifting, carrying, falling objects, machinery, roadside work, height, sealants and site assessment
f: Glass-sector injuries commonly arise during handling, lifting and carrying.
Moving, flying or falling glass and objects are significant hazards.
Contact with moving machinery is a main cause of injury.
Broken glass and cutting tools can cause serious cuts.
Large vehicle glazing can weigh up to about 100 kilograms and require handling aids or team methods.
Glazing work can involve work at height and difficult access.
Sealants and related products require chemical exposure controls.
Mobile glazing technicians need training to assess changing roadside, weather and site conditions.
families.g: Glass-handling risk depends on pane size, mass and condition, sharp edges and breakage, lifting method, machinery and tools, access and height, environment, chemicals and worker competence.

families.s: HSE glass and glazing dust, fume and occupational-asthma control guidance
families.t: glass cutting, laminated glass, methylated spirits, dust, fumes, asthma, local exhaust ventilation, cleaning and surveillance
f: Glass cutting can produce dust that presents respiratory risk.
Methylated spirits used in laminated-glass cutting can contribute to inhalation exposure.
Dusts and fumes can cause long-term health problems including asthma.
Local exhaust ventilation can greatly reduce exposure where dust or fume is generated.
Work methods and tools should minimise airborne dust and vapour at source.
Cleaning should avoid dry sweeping or compressed-air methods that redistribute contamination.
COSHH assessment should cover products, process emissions, exposure routes and maintenance tasks.
Health surveillance may be appropriate where a recognised respiratory risk remains after controls.
families.g: Glass respiratory risk depends on cutting and machining method, dust and solvent generation, enclosure and extraction, cleaning, task duration, PPE, surveillance and worker susceptibility.

families.s: HSE food-processing machinery safeguarding and cleaning guidance
families.t: conveyors, guarding, interlocks, food machinery standards, cutting, mixing, packaging, cleaning, maintenance and intervention
f: Food and drink machinery accidents frequently involve conveyors and other processing machines.
A substantial proportion of investigated injuries involved failures to guard main danger areas.
Safeguards may use safe design, fixed guards or hinged and removable interlocked guards.
Food machinery standards cover meat, fish, dairy, bakery, catering, packaging and other equipment.
Cleaning access should be designed so hygienic cleaning does not require unsafe exposure to moving parts.
Jams, blockages and product changes require defined safe intervention methods.
Maintenance should test guards, interlocks, emergency stops and control systems.
Machine selection and retrofit decisions should reflect current standards and foreseeable use.
families.g: Food-machinery risk depends on machine class and movement, product and cleaning needs, access and intervention, guarding and interlocks, controls, isolation, maintenance and competence.

families.s: HSE food-industry hand-knife and sharp-tool injury prevention guidance
families.t: knife selection, sharpening, hand position, falling tools, storage, protective gloves and aprons, training and supervision
f: Hand knives are an important source of struck-by and cutting injuries in food manufacture.
Knife tasks include cutting, boning, jointing, trussing and evisceration.
The knife should be suitable for the product, task and worker.
Sharp, well-maintained knives can reduce excessive force and loss of control.
Work layout and technique should keep the free hand and body out of the cutting path.
Knives should be stored and carried so exposed blades cannot injure people.
Cut-resistant gloves, arm guards, aprons or other protection should match the knife hazard.
Training and supervision should cover selection, sharpening, use, cleaning, storage and disposal of damaged knives.
families.g: Knife risk depends on blade and product, force and direction, hand and body position, work pace, sharpness and maintenance, storage, PPE, training and supervision.

families.s: HSE meat, poultry and fish processing occupational-health guidance
families.t: machinery, noise, cold, microorganisms, aerosol proteins, PAHs, respiratory disease, skin exposure and surveillance
f: Meat, poultry and fish processing uses conveyors, bandsaws, derinders, skinning and packaging machinery.
Powered saws, chillers, bowl choppers and packaging equipment can create harmful noise.
Long-term work in reduced temperatures can cause health and comfort problems.
Poultry processing can expose workers to microorganisms such as Campylobacter or Salmonella.
Fish-processing aerosol proteins can cause occupational asthma.
Smoking meat or fish can create exposure to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
Controls should combine machinery safeguarding, ventilation, hygiene, temperature management and PPE.
Health surveillance and prompt reporting should address respiratory, skin, hearing and musculoskeletal symptoms.
families.g: Meat, poultry and fish risk depends on machinery and knives, noise, biological agents and proteins, smoke and chemicals, cold, wet work, work pace, hygiene, ventilation and surveillance.
